It is a first-generation H1 antihistamine that is widely used as a generic, over-the-counter medication to treat allergies. 
When exceeding approved doses, diphenhydramine produces powerful deliriant effects.
Diphenhydramine was first synthesized in 1943. 
In 1946, it became the first prescription antihistamine approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. It was approved for over-the-counter use in the 1980s. 
Today, it is typically used to treat allergies, but it may also be used for several conditions, including itchiness, insomnia, motion sickness, nausea, and the symptoms of Parkinson's disease. 
Subjective effects include sedation, anxiety, tactile hallucinations, memory suppression, thought disorganization, dysphoria, and external hallucinations. Lower doses tend to produce a stoning, body-high effect, while higher doses produce a state of delirium in which the user sees and hears fully-formed, compelling hallucinations. Doses between these two points are uncomfortable and dysphoric. 
Notably, it is frequently reported to produce significant nausea and bodily discomfort ("body load"). Most people who try diphenhydramine do not report positive effects and do not wish to repeat the experience.
It is generally considered to have low abuse potential due to its dysphoric effects. The toxicity of recreational use is not well-studied. Anecdotal reports suggest that chronic use (i.e., high dose, repeated administration) may cause persisting hallucinations and impairments in cognition & memory. High doses have also been linked to seizures and cardiotoxicity.
It is highly advised to use harm reduction practices if using this substance.

Modafinil (also known by the brand names Provigil, Alertec, Modavigil, and others) is a eugeroic substance of the benzhydryl class that produces wakefulness-promoting and stimulant effects when administered. It is commonly used to enhance cognition, reduce fatigue, and increase alertness in both medical and non-medical contexts.
Modafinil is approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea, shift work sleep disorder and narcolepsy. However, studies have shown that modafinil may also be useful off-label for alleviating the symptoms of depression, bipolar disorder, Parkinson's disease, seasonal depressive disorder, ADHD, and various other conditions which have fatigue as a symptom. 
Modafinil has also been used as a doping agent by various athletes due to its ability to produce physical stimulation. It has recently gained mainstream popularity for its use as a "smart drug" to improve memory, counteract the desire or need for sleep, and increase general productivity.

β-Phenyl-γ-aminobutyric acid (also known as Fenibut, Phenybut, Noofen, Citrocard, and commonly as Phenibut) is a lesser-known depressant substance of the gabapentinoid class. 
Phenibut acts as a receptor agonist for GABA, the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. 
It is chemically related to baclofen, pregabalin, and gabapentin.
Phenibut was developed in the Soviet Union in the 1960s, where it has been used as a pharmaceutical drug to treat a wide variety of conditions, including post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, depression, asthenia, insomnia, alcoholism, stuttering, and vestibular disorders, and others. In the rest of the world, phenibut is not approved for clinical use and is instead sold as a nutritional supplement. 
Subjective effects include anxiety suppression, sedation, muscle relaxation, enhanced motivation, and euphoria. Lower doses (under 1 gram) are typically used as a cognitive and lifestyle supplement while higher doses are used for a recreational high that is reported to be subjectively similar to GHB, alcohol, and certain benzodiazepines. 
Although phenibut is commonly marketed as a nootropic by retailers, evidence that it enhances cognition is limited. It is generally accepted that phenibut has anxiolytic effects in both animal and in humans. Due to its habit-forming properties, it is highly advised to use harm reduction practices if using this substance.

mechanism.text:
Phenibut has a more complex pharmacology than many other depressants. Unlike the benzodiazepines, phenibut acts as a full agonist at GABAB receptors, similar to baclofen and high-dose GHB. At higher doses phenibut loses its selectivity for GABAB and gains additional activity as a GABAA agonist. Phenibut's action at GABAB receptors is responsible for its sedative effects.

Recent research has shown that phenibut binds to and blocks voltage-dependent calcium channels (VDCCs) containing the α2δ subunit, like the gabapentinoids gabapentin and pregabalin. Both enantiomers of phenibut show this action with similar efficacy. The R-enantiomer has five times greater affinity for α2δ-containing voltage-gated calcium channels than for GABAB receptors, while the S-enantiomer has no efficacy at GABAB receptors.

Phenibut's analgesic effects in rodents are mediated not by GABAB receptors but by blockade of α2δ-containing voltage-gated calcium channels.

description.text:
Disclaimer: The dosage information on this website has been compiled from user reports and other resources for educational purposes only and does not constitute a recommendation; accuracy should be verified against additional sources.

Methylnaphthidate (also known as HDMP-28) is a novel synthetic stimulant of the substituted benzylpiperidine chemical class. It is a structural analog of methylphenidate (e.g., Ritalin, Concerta), a drug commonly used in the treatment of ADHD, and produces moderate stimulant effects upon administration.

Like other members of the benzylpiperidine class, methylnaphthidate is generally believed to act as a monoamine reuptake inhibitor. However, reports indicate that its subjective effects differ noticeably from those of conventional dopaminergic stimulants. This may be related to its apparently more pronounced inhibition of serotonin reuptake, a property not typically associated with standard methylphenidate analogs.

Very little data currently exists on the pharmacological properties, metabolism, and toxicity of methylnaphthidate, and it has virtually no history of human use. It is sometimes commercially sold by online vendors as a gray-market research chemical, alongside other methylphenidate analogs such as ethylphenidate, isopropylphenidate, and 4F-MPH. Anyone who chooses to use this insufficiently studied stimulant should exercise considerable caution and adopt appropriate harm reduction practices.

mechanism.text: Methylnaphthidate is believed to act primarily as a monoamine triple reuptake inhibitor—that is, it binds to and partially blocks the transporter proteins normally responsible for clearing dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin from the synaptic cleft, effectively elevating levels of these neurotransmitters throughout the brain and central nervous system. This leads to an accumulation of these molecules in the brain, particularly within reward pathways, producing stimulant and euphoric effects.

description.text: Psilocybe caerulipes is a potent psychedelic mushroom within the genus Psilocybe. Research has shown that the fruiting bodies of Psilocybe caerulipes contain several distinct indole alkaloids, including psilocybin, psilocin, and baeocystin.

Nymphaea nouchali var. caerulea (Commonly known as Blue Lotus) is a water lily found throughout most of the eastern half of Africa.

The flower has been used for over 2000 years in teas, herbal blends and in perfumes. 
Like other species in the genus, the plant contains the psychoactive alkaloid aporphine which is thought to be the main constituent causing the effects of the flower, however, it is more likely a group of aporphine alkaloids are working in conjunction to create the various effects as opposed to just aporphine. High potent extracts when ingested or smoked in high doses are reported to produce euphoria and hallucinations.

mechanism.text:
Aporphine is considered the primary active constituent; it is a dopamine receptor agonist acting at both D1 and D2 receptors. Nuciferine is another important alkaloid: it acts as an antagonist at 5-HT2A, 5-HT, and 5-HT receptors while simultaneously acting as a partial agonist at D2, D5, and 5-HT receptors, and as a full agonist at 5-HT and D4 receptors. It also inhibits the dopamine transporter (DAT).

The effects of blue lotus are produced by a group of alkaloids known as the aporphines. This class contains numerous dopamine agonists, a broad range of serotonin antagonists and agonists, and various reuptake inhibitors. Apomorphine, the active metabolite of aporphine, shares a catechol structure similar to that of dopamine.

description.text: Psilocybe is a genus of gilled mushrooms found throughout the world. The genus is best known for the species within it that possess psychedelic properties. Psilocin and psilocybin are the primary psychedelic compounds responsible for the subjective effects produced by many species within the genus.

N-Acetyl-5-methoxytryptamine (also known as melatonin) is a hormone of the tryptamine class. It is found in animals, plants, fungi, and bacteria. In animals, it functions as a hormone that anticipates the daily onset of darkness; it may have different functions in other organisms.
Melatonin is active and can be taken sublingually and buccally by placing it into one's mouth and allowing it to absorb over a period of 15-25 minutes. It is less active when taken orally. 
Melatonin is commonly used as a medication for insomnia; however, there is insufficient scientific evidence to prove any benefit in this area. It is sold over-the-counter in most pharmacies within the United States and Canada. In other countries, it may require a prescription or not be available.
It should be noted that when purchasing melatonin, dosages may range from 3 - 10mg. While not dangerous, this dosage range is well beyond the effective dose of .25 mg, and may increase instances of drowsiness the next day.

Amanita pantherina, also known as the panther cap or false blusher (owing to its resemblance to the edible blusher mushroom), is a psychoactive mushroom belonging to the genus Amanita. The primary psychoactive constituent of this mushroom is muscimol. Its subjective effects are not similar to those of psilocybin mushrooms.

Psilocybin mushrooms (also known as magic mushrooms, psychedelic mushrooms, and shrooms) are a family of psychoactive fungi that contain psilocybin, a psychedelic substance of the tryptamine class. The mechanism of action is not fully known, although binding activity at serotonin receptors is thought to be involved.
Psilocybin mushrooms occur on all continents and have been taxonomically classified into over 200 species, the most potent of which belong to the genus Psilocybe. Based on imagery found in prehistoric rock art, they are thought to have been used by various human cultures since before recorded history. 
After being introduced to the Western world in the 1950s, they generated substantial public interest.  Along with LSD, they were incorporated into the youth counterculture movement of the 1960s. Widespread usage of psychedelics provoked a societal backlash, and they were prohibited in 1970.
Today, they are among the most widely used psychedelic substances (partly due to the ease of personal cultivation and harvesting). As a part of the so-called "psychedelic renaissance", they are currently being investigated in the treatment of a number of ailments including anxiety, depression, addiction, and other mental disorders.
Subjective effects include visual geometry, hallucinatory states, time distortion, enhanced introspection, conceptual thinking, euphoria, and ego loss. The intensity and duration of effects can vary greatly depending on factors such as species and batch, which can complicate standardized dosing information (see this section). They are often described to evoke entheogenic, mystical-like, or transpersonal experiences that may facilitate self-reflection and personal growth. 
In distinction to psychedelics like LSD, mescaline, and 2C-B, which may be described as "stimulating", "cerebral", and "bright", psilocybin mushrooms are typically described as having an "earthy", "subliminal", or "dream-like" quality. They also are reported to produce slightly more emotion enhancement, time distortion and ego loss than the aforementioned substances, as well as more nausea, confusion, and sedation.
Unlike most highly prohibited substances, psilocybin mushrooms have low abuse potential and are neither addictive nor physiologically toxic. However, adverse psychological reactions such as severe anxiety, paranoia, delusions and psychosis are always possible, particularly among individuals predisposed to mental disorders. 
It is highly advised to use harm reduction practices if using this substance.

4-HO-DPT (also known as 4-hydroxy-N,N-dipropyltryptamine and sometimes referred to as Procin) is a psychedelic substance of the tryptamine class. Alexander Shulgin first synthesized 4-HO-DPT and documented it in his book TiHKAL (Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved). It is the 4-hydroxyl analog of DPT.
Today it is either used recreationally or as an entheogenic compound and is typically acquired through the use of online research chemical vendors. Due to the difficulty of its synthesis, it remains relatively uncommon even for a substituted tryptamine and has very little history of human usage.

Choline is a chemical substance which serves as a precursor to the neurotransmitter acetylcholine in the brain. Choline is an essential nutrient in humans, with documented roles in reducing the risk of neural tube defects, fatty liver disease and other pathologies. It is also used in the synthesis of components in cell membranes. Choline is rarely sold as a free base; it is generally combined with an acid to form a salt such as choline bitartrate for stability, or conjugated into one of the more complex forms such as citicoline.
Choline supplementation can be used in the treatment of liver disorders, hepatitis, glaucoma, atherosclerosis, Alzheimer's disease, bipolar disorder and possibly other neurological disorders. It has also been shown to have a positive effect on those suffering from alcoholism. 
When taken as a supplement, this compound has been reported to produce nootropic effects. It is easily available and commonly sold for this purpose through the use of online supplement vendors.

mechanism.text:
Choline and its metabolites serve three primary physiological functions:

Phospholipid synthesis. Choline is necessary for the production of various phospholipids, which form cell membranes and signaling lipid rafts. Neural lipid rafts are receiving increasing attention in the field of psychiatry. Cholinergic neurotransmission, as a precursor to acetylcholine synthesis. Choline supplementation may allow acetylcholine to accumulate to higher levels than would otherwise occur. Since acetylcholine is involved in memory function, this may explain the nootropic effects. [citation needed] Production of trimethylamine (betaine). Trimethylamine is necessary for osmoregulation and is also involved in the synthesis of SAM-e.

description.text:
Ethanol (also known as ethyl alcohol, ethyl hydroxide, drinking alcohol or simply alcohol) is a depressant substance of the alcohol class. It is the primary psychoactive component of alcoholic drinks, liquors and spirits; making it the second-most widely used recreational substance globally (after caffeine). The alcoholic beverage known as beer is the most widely consumed beverage in the world after water and tea. Ethanol principally acts by binding to GABA receptors in parts of the brain, but is also known to exhibit “promiscuous” pharmacological activity due to its activation of and/or interaction with various neurotransmitters and receptor sites.
Ethanol is only one of several alcohols; other alcohols such as methanol and isopropyl alcohol are significantly more toxic. A mild, brief exposure to isopropyl alcohol (which is only moderately more toxic than ethanol) is unlikely to cause any serious harm, but methanol is lethal even in small quantities, as little as 10–15 milliliters (2–3 teaspoons).  However, isopropyl alcohol, and ethanol, are just a few psychoactive alcohols in alcoholic drinks, and analogues. Unlike primary alcohols like ethanol, tertiary alcohols cannot be oxidized into aldehyde or carboxylic acid metabolites, which are often toxic. For example, the tertiary alcohol 2M2B is  20 times more potent than ethanol, and has been used recreationally.
The practice of consuming ethanol in the form of alcoholic drinks predates written history. Alcoholic beverages have been produced and consumed by humans since the Neolithic Era, from hunter-gatherer communities to nation-states. In modern times, drinking alcohol is the most commonly used legal recreational substance in the world. More than 100 countries have laws regulating its production, sale, and consumption.
Subjective effects include sedation, disinhibition, anxiety suppression, empathy, affection and sociability enhancement, muscle relaxation, and euphoria. However, the degree to which these effects are present can depend somewhat on the method of production and degree of distillation. Alcoholic beverages are divided into three major classes: beers, wines, and spirits (distilled beverages).
Despite sometimes being considered harmless on basis of its legality and widespread use, ethanol is capable of causing significant harm and toxicity to the user. It is considered to have moderate abuse potential and chronic use is associated with escalating tolerance, physical dependence, and addiction. Additionally, chronic use is associated with negative effects on the brain and other organs. There is also a substantial risk of fatal respiratory overdose when it is combined with other depressants (e.g. benzodiazepines, opioids). As a result, it is highly advised to use harm reduction practices if using this substance.

Tyrosine (also known as L-Tyrosine and 4-hydroxyphenylalanine) is a non-essential amino acid that serves a precursor to dopamine, adrenaline and norepinephrine in the human body. As a supplement, it is reported to act as a mild stimulant. It is also one of the 22 amino acids that are used by cells to synthesize proteins and is abundant in many high-protein foods, such as chicken, turkey, fish, cottage cheese, cheese, yogurt, almonds, milk, avocados, bananas, peanuts, pumpkin seeds, sesame seeds and soy products.
Some evidence suggests tyrosine supplementation can affect performance on working memory tasks under certain conditions, especially stress. Tyrosine may enhance convergent (double-task) thinking. In one study, tyrosine even seemed to reverse some of the detrimental effects of sleep deprivation on cognitive performance. However, if tyrosine increases working memory performance by elevating catecholamine levels, the effect could easily be short-lived. Some animal studies have shown dopamine levels quickly return to baseline.

mechanism.text:
The effects produced by tyrosine as a supplement or psychoactive compound arise from its role as a precursor to the catecholamine neurotransmitters. Supplemental L-tyrosine is converted in the body to L-DOPA, which is subsequently decarboxylated to dopamine, then further converted to norepinephrine, and finally to epinephrine. This means it does raise the levels of these neurotransmitters in the brain, producing stimulant and euphoric effects. These three neurotransmitters are collectively referred to as "catecholamines."

The synthesis of catecholamines in the body is limited by the local substrate pool, so the subjective effects of tyrosine tend to reach a "ceiling" at high doses, beyond which further supplementation for the purpose of enhancing stimulation typically becomes ineffective.

Beyond its role as a proteinogenic amino acid, tyrosine has additional functions owing to its phenolic hydroxyl group. It is found in proteins involved in signal transduction processes, where it acts as a phosphate group acceptor from protein kinases. Phosphorylation of the hydroxyl group can alter the activity of the target protein or serve as part of a signaling cascade through SH2 domain binding.

description.text:
Amantadine is a hallucinogen and weak stimulant of the adamantane class that produces lasting dissociative and delirious effects upon administration. It is a derivative of adamantane and is pharmacologically related to compounds such as memantine, rimantadine, and adapromine.

Amantadine was originally synthesized in the 1960s as an antiviral agent for the treatment of influenza. In 1969, it was serendipitously discovered that amantadine possessed central dopaminergic stimulant-like properties, and it was subsequently introduced for the treatment of Parkinson's disease owing to its ability to increase dopamine levels in the brain.

mechanism.text:
Amantadine is a weak NMDA receptor antagonist (Ki = 10 µM) that increases dopamine release and blocks dopamine reuptake. It also inhibits nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs).

Amantadine has been found to bind to and act as an agonist at the σ1 receptor (Ki = 7.44 µM), and activation of the σ1 receptor has been implicated in the dopaminergic effects.

The antiviral and psychoactive mechanisms of action of amantadine are unrelated. The mechanism underlying amantadine's antiviral activity involves interference with the viral protein M2, a proton channel.

description.text: Lophophora fricii (also known as false peyote) is a cactus belonging to the genus Lophophora. It contains relatively high concentrations of pellotine and anhalonidine, but low concentrations of mescaline. Habermann (1978a) reported that a cultivated specimen of L. fricii was non-hallucinogenic at a dose of 3 g/kg.

Alprazolam (also known as Xanax) is a depressant substance of the benzodiazepine class. Its characteristic effects include anxiety suppression, sedation, disinhibition, and muscle relaxation. 
Like other benzodiazepines, alprazolam binds to specific sites on the GABAA receptor. It is commonly used for the medical treatment of panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), or social anxiety disorder (SAD).
Alprazolam has a fast onset of action and symptomatic relief. 90% of peak effects are achieved within the 1st hour of using in preparation for panic disorder and full peak effects are achieved in 1.5 and 1.6 hours respectively. Peak benefits achieved for GAD may take up to a week.
The sudden discontinuation of benzodiazepines can be potentially dangerous or life-threatening for individuals using regularly for extended periods of time, sometimes resulting in seizures or death. It is highly recommended to taper one's dose by gradually lowering the amount taken each day for a prolonged period of time instead of stopping abruptly.

(R)-Modafinil (also known as armodafinil, with brand names including Nuvigil, Artvigil, and Waklert) is a eugeroic of the benzhydryl class. Armodafinil is the enantiopure preparation of modafinil (brand name Provigil). Unlike the racemic preparation, which contains 50% each of the (S)- and (R)-enantiomers, armodafinil consists only of modafinil's (R)-enantiomer.

Armodafinil was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in June 2007 to treat obstructive sleep apnea, shift work sleep disorder, and narcolepsy.

Besides promoting wakefulness and increasing locomotor activity in animals, armodafinil may produce rewarding psychoactive and euphoric effects, such as changes in mood, perception, thinking, and feeling, which are also commonly seen in humans with other central nervous system stimulants.

A study that gave patients modafinil, methylphenidate, and placebo found that armodafinil produces "psychoactive and euphoric effects and feelings consistent with methylphenidate". Compared with modafinil, armodafinil reaches peak plasma concentration later after administration, so it may be somewhat more effective at improving wakefulness in patients with excessive daytime sleepiness.

mechanism.text:
Although the exact mechanism by which modafinil and its R-enantiomer armodafinil reduce sleepiness has not been fully elucidated, available evidence suggests they promote wakefulness by acting directly or indirectly on several components of the sleep/wake circuitry. Modafinil and armodafinil are thought to inhibit GABA and to promote the activity of dopamine, norepinephrine, histamine, and orexin/hypocretin.

Modafinil and armodafinil both raise norepinephrine (NE) and dopamine (DA) levels, possibly by blocking both the NE and DA reuptake transporters (NET and DAT). The action of NE at α-adrenergic receptors and of DA at dopamine D2 receptors is thought to contribute jointly to modafinil's wakefulness-promoting properties. Orexin is a key component of the arousal system, so modafinil's presumed action on the orexinergic system may help increase alertness. Modafinil may also indirectly raise histamine levels by reducing GABAergic inhibition of histaminergic neurons or by acting on orexinergic neurons. Raised histamine may contribute both to modafinil's wakefulness-promoting effect and to its potential to increase alertness.

In genetically engineered mice lacking the dopamine transporter (DAT), modafinil lost its wakefulness-promoting activity, which suggests that this activity depends on DAT. However, unlike that of amphetamine, modafinil's wakefulness-promoting effect is not attenuated in rats by the dopamine receptor antagonist haloperidol. In addition, α-methyl-p-tyrosine, a dopamine synthesis inhibitor, blocks the effects of amphetamine but not the locomotor activity induced by modafinil.

description.text: Atropa belladonna, commonly known as belladonna or deadly nightshade, is a plant of the family Solanaceae, native to Europe, North Africa, and Western Asia. It contains tropane substances that are deliriants. Both its leaves and berries are highly toxic and contain tropane alkaloids, including atropine, scopolamine, and hyoscyamine. These toxins produce bizarre delirium and hallucinations (similar to those produced by Datura) and are also used as medicinal anticholinergic agents.

Peganum harmala, commonly called Syrian rue, harmel, espand, esfand, wild rue, African rue, or aspand, is a plant native to the eastern Iranian region west to India. It has also spread invasively throughout Arizona, California, Montana, Nevada, Oregon, Texas and Washington. The plant itself produces seeds which contain harmala alkaloids and is easily accessible and legal to purchase online.

Ibotenic acid or (S)-2-amino-2-(3-hydroxyisoxazol-5-yl)acetic acid (also referred to as ibotenate) is a psychoactive substance which occurs naturally in Amanita muscaria and related species of mushrooms. It is an analogue of the neurotransmitter glutamate, and due to its structural similarity to this neurotransmitter, acts as a non-selective glutamate receptor agonist.
Ibotenic acid is a powerful neurotoxin, and has been employed as a "brain-lesioning agent" through cranial injections in scientific research conducted in rats. The same properties have not been studied in humans, however it could very well be a human neurotoxin as well.

Tabernanthe iboga, or simply iboga, is a perennial tropical rainforest shrub native to western Central Africa and a psychedelic. In parts of Africa where it grows, the root bark is chewed for various pharmacological or ritual purposes. Its psychoactive alkaloid ibogaine is also used in the treatment of substance use disorders and depression. Voacanga africana also contains small amounts of ibogaine and ibogaine precursors.

Mescaline (also known as 3,4,5-trimethoxyphenethylamine) is a naturally occurring classical psychedelic of the phenethylamine class. It is found naturally in the peyote cactus (Lophophora williamsii), the San Pedro cactus (Echinopsis pachanoi), the Peruvian torch cactus (Echinopsis peruviana), and within the Cactaceae and Fabaceae plant families. It is one of the oldest known psychedelics and the parent compound of the psychedelic phenethylamines, one of the two main subclasses of psychedelic compounds (the other being the tryptamines).

Mescaline was first isolated from the peyote cactus in 1897 by the German chemist Arthur Heffter. Indigenous peoples of Mexico have used peyote ritually for at least 5,700 years, and other mescaline-containing cacti such as San Pedro have a long history of use throughout South America, from Peru to Ecuador. Mescaline was a central focus of the life's work of American chemist Alexander Shulgin, who used it as a starting point for the synthesis of dozens of novel psychedelic compounds, documented in his 1991 book PiHKAL ("Phenethylamines I Have Known and Loved").

Subjective effects include open- and closed-eye visuals, time distortion, increased introspection, conceptual thinking, euphoria, and ego dissolution. Mescaline is generally considered one of the gentlest, most insightful, and most euphoric psychedelics. It is well known for placing more emphasis on physical and tactile sensations than tryptamine-class psychedelics such as psilocybin or DMT (sometimes compared to MDMA), the latter of which tend toward more chaotic mindscapes and more dynamically active visual geometry. Its rich, organic, and complex character has led to its being regarded as one of the premier substances for psychedelic therapy. Synthetic mescaline is highly sought after by connoisseurs, but owing to its low potency and relatively high production costs it is typically available only in limited quantities.

Unlike other heavily prohibited substances, mescaline has not been demonstrated to be physiologically toxic or habit-forming. However, adverse psychological reactions such as anxiety, delusions, illusions, and psychosis are still possible, particularly in individuals predisposed to mental illness. It should also be noted that in street markets, terms such as "mescaline" or "synthetic mescaline" are frequently used as deceptive labels for other psychedelics — such as 2C-x, DOx, or 25x-NBOMe — which are generally more dangerous. Harm reduction practices are strongly recommended if these substances are used.

mechanism.text: Mescaline acts similarly to other psychedelics. It binds to and activates the serotonin 5-HT2A receptor with high affinity. How activation of the 5-HT2A receptor produces a psychedelic state is not fully understood, but it likely involves excitation of neurons in the prefrontal cortex. Mescaline is also known to bind to and activate the serotonin 5-HT2C receptor.

description.text:
Ephedrine is a naturally occurring central nervous system stimulant obtained from the plant Ephedra equisetina. It is commonly used as a stimulant, attention aid, decongestant, and appetite suppressant. It is frequently used to prevent hypotension during spinal anesthesia.

Ephedrine is closely related in structure to methamphetamine and pseudoephedrine, although its central nervous system effects are considerably weaker and longer-lasting than those of amphetamine-class compounds. Its peripheral stimulant effects resemble those of epinephrine, though it is less potent than epinephrine, the hormone produced by the adrenal gland in the body.

mechanism.text:
The primary mechanism of action of ephedrine involves increasing the activity of catecholamines at α, β1, and β2 adrenergic receptors. It also acts as an NDRA (norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent).

Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic amine that acts on the sympathetic nervous system (SNS). The primary mechanism of action relies on its ability to indirectly stimulate the adrenergic receptor system by increasing norepinephrine activity at postsynaptic α and β receptors. Whether direct interaction with α receptors occurs is considered unlikely but remains a matter of debate. L-Ephedrine, and in particular its stereoisomer norpseudoephedrine (also found in khat), exerts indirect sympathomimetic effects; owing to its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier, it is a CNS stimulant similar to amphetamine but less pronounced, as it releases norepinephrine and dopamine in the substantia nigra.

Compared with norephedrine, the presence of the N-methyl group reduces binding affinity at α receptors. Nevertheless, ephedrine binds better than N-methylephedrine, which carries an additional methyl group on the nitrogen atom. The spatial orientation of the hydroxyl group is also important for receptor binding and functional activity.

description.text:
Salvinorin B methoxymethyl ether (2-O-methoxymethyl salvinorin B, or 2-MMSB) is a semisynthetic analogue of the natural product salvinorin B, prepared for scientific research. Compared with salvinorin A, whose duration of action is under 30 minutes, it has a longer duration of approximately 2 to 3 hours and a higher affinity and potency at the κ-opioid receptor. Like the related compound herkinorin, salvinorin B methoxymethyl ether is prepared from salvinorin B; the most convenient preparation of salvinorin B is by deacetylation of salvinorin A, since although both salvinorin A and salvinorin B are present in Salvia divinorum, salvinorin A is present in higher concentrations.

Salvinorin B methoxymethyl ether has a Ki of 0.60 nM at the κ-opioid receptor and is approximately five times more potent than salvinorin A in animal studies, though it is still roughly half as potent as its more powerful homologue salvinorin B ethoxymethyl ether.

Salvinorin A is the main active psychoactive molecule within Salvia Divinorum, a Mexican plant which has a long history of use as an entheogen by indigenous Mazatec shamans. It is structurally distinct from other naturally occurring hallucinogens (such as DMT, psilocin and mescaline) because it contains no nitrogen atoms, making it a terpenoid and not an alkaloid as is the norm. This means it cannot be rendered as a salt. 
It also differs in subjective experience compared to other hallucinogens, and has been described as an atypical psychedelic although this formal classification is debatable.
